title: Where Solana verification tooling is weaker, the framework substitutes cross-verification between signers
content:
A.2.11.1.3.2.2.2.2.3.4 makes an unusual admission for a security policy: "[v]erification tooling for SVM Multisig transactions is currently more limited than for EVM environments. Signers should exercise additional caution and may cross-verify transactions with other signers prior to execution."

Most frameworks state uniform requirements and let reality diverge silently. Naming the asymmetry is more useful, because it tells signers *where* their tooling is weakest rather than letting them assume equal assurance across chains — and misplaced confidence is the actual risk when the same person signs on both.

The substitute is social. Where a simulator or a decoder cannot independently confirm a transaction, two signers reasoning about it separately is the remaining check. That is a real control — independent review catches errors — but it is weaker than machine verification and it consumes the scarce commodity in emergency operations: signer time.

The SVM requirements themselves are correspondingly more manual. A.2.11.1.3.2.2.2.2.3.1 asks signers to verify "the sender, recipient addresses, asset type, transfer amounts, configuration changes, and associated instructions" and to confirm "that no unauthorized interactions are included" — an enumeration check on a full instruction list, done by eye, where the EVM path has decoded calldata and simulation to lean on.

The honest reading is that multi-chain expansion carries an uneven security cost, and the Atlas prices it in caution rather than pretending parity.
description: The Atlas states plainly that SVM multisig tooling lags EVM and responds by asking signers to exercise additional caution and check transactions with each other before execution.
